#1557. The climate is in crisis — here’s four things we can do

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Projections of future climate change show a relatively cooler world thanks to the growth of renewable energy. And yet the world is still on track to reach around 2.6˚C of warming by the end of the century — far beyond what many climate scientists say we need to avoid the worst impacts of climate change. So, what are we going to do about it?

In the second episode of Cooked? I talk to experts around the world about their big ideas of what we can do to tackle climate change. We talk about energy, food, economics and how the world needs to adapt to a warmer world.

04:27 The synergistic solutions to climate change and other big challenges

12:03 Can we end humanity’s addiction to meat?

21:49 How to make economics work to fight climate change

How countries can grow without impoverishing future generations

Nick Petrić Howe: And then one final question, super easy one, what do we need to do to save the world?

Hannah Ritchie: Haha, oh that’s a tough one

Nick Petrić Howe: When it comes to climate, there’s one thing that’s been on my mind for a long time. What are we supposed to do about it? Saving the world isn’t quite as easy as it looks in movies. You can’t just blow-up climate change and then walk coolly off into the distance.

But after the last episode of this series, it did feel like things were a bit more positive than I had previously thought. Renewable energy and electrification are making a dent in our emissions. But, the other thing that was clear was that simply relying on renewables won’t be enough and even that progress needs to move more quickly. So, I was interested in some of the big ideas that are out there. What other ways can we well… save the world?

So, I asked a lot of different experts that exact question. Their answers ranged from the nuanced...

Eoin McLaughlin: What do we want to achieve, right? Is ultimately what the question should be. Is like, well, what kind of society do we want to have? Do we want to have one that is, you know, prosperous in the future? Or do we just want to focus on what's going on day-to-day within the political cycle.

Nick Petrić Howe: In fairness, I didn't actually expect an answer. If there were easy answers, we’d have done it already. Silver bullets are great for werewolves, but they rarely exist for huge global issues. But that didn’t stop me from wanting to know what we should do.

I'm Nick Petrić Howe and this is Cooked? a podcast miniseries for Nature where I try and figure out whether there's still hope in the battle against climate change or whether we're well… cooked.

In this episode, I'm going to try and find out some of the big ideas to try and counter climate change. And I knew exactly where to start.

Hannah Ritchie: What I wanted to do is to look at the data and understand if we want to solve these problems, what are the really key and big things that we need to do to solve them?

Nick Petrić Howe: If you tuned into the previous episode, you’ll know that I was feeling pretty down about the climate. To my mind, not enough was being done and what was being done wasn’t going far enough. So I kinda was wondering if we’re well… a bit fucked?

But I learnt last time that maybe I was being a bit pessimistic. And one of the people I spoke to had a lot to say on this, along with a lot of data to back themselves up. It turned out they also had some big ideas to go along with this.

Hannah Ritchie: Humans actually are capable of solving problems when we put resources behind it, where we really get our act together and work on it. And that obviously has spillovers for climate. you know, I think it is possible for us to tackle this.

Nick Petrić Howe: This is Hannah Ritchie, who you may remember from the last episode. She is a data scientist at Our World in Data and the University of Oxford and has written a book about how we can solve seven key environmental problems, including climate change.

Like the quotes from the start, there are nuanced or simplistic ways to think about solving climate change. On the face of it all that we need to do is stop emitting carbon. That is obviously not quite so straightforward, especially because... climate change isn’t the only problem we have.

Climate change regularly comes up in polls as a big concern, but when compared to other issues people tend to be more anxious about more immediate worries, like the cost of living, the economy and crime. With only finite resources and energy, climate change can fade into the background.

But by looking at the data, Hannah has found that there are ways to tackle climate change and other issues.

Hannah Ritchie: So, if you take the example of climate change and air pollution, the root of basically both of those problems is burning stuff, right? And either that's burning wood or biomass, so indoor air pollution is still a huge issue for people and actually is linked to energy poverty. So millions of people still die from indoor air pollution or outdoor air pollution — basically the burning of fossil fuels. The core solution there is to basically move away from burning stuff and primarily burning fossil fuels. Increasingly we have good alternatives, low-carbon and cleaner alternatives to these sources.

Nick Petrić Howe: This isn’t to say there aren’t trade-offs to any particular solution, there are still potential downsides that would need to be managed, but the point is that there are ways to tackle climate change and tackle other problems people care about.

To take the example of air pollution, one key outdoor pollutant is sulphur dioxide; this primarily gets in the air from burning of oil or coal and can make it hard to breathe. So, using less oil or coal can reduce this kind of air pollution and benefit the climate. Billions of people worldwide are also exposed to indoor air pollution, which comes from burning of wood, kerosene or coal indoors. A shift to electric or gas heating and cooking would also make people’s homes healthier and send fewer warming emissions out into the world.

Transitions, though, can be tricky. In China, for example, in an effort to reduce air pollution, using coal has been banned in some places, even though some people can’t afford the alternatives, like gas heating.

At the societal level, this would still benefit people’s health and the climate, and alternatives would come down in price. And Hannah thinks that the data can guide us towards the decisions that may bring the most benefits. But she also cautions against looking for the ‘perfect solution’.

Hannah Ritchie: So, I think it's often the case that when we're thinking about any of the alternatives to the current system we have, whether that's solar power or wind or electric vehicles or plant-based substitutes, I think we often have this challenge that we're on the hunt for the ultimate solution that has zero downsides, right? And by zero downsides, I mean, you don't need no mining for it. The land-use is very low or basically zero. There are zero repercussions or knock-on impacts whatsoever. And think the reality is if that's the kind of solution that we're waiting for to appear, it's not going to. And the reality is that that stops us actually moving forward and taking action because we're waiting for it. And the reality is we'll just wait on a current system which is mostly running on fossil fuels.

Nick Petrić Howe: You can see this kind of thinking play out with electric cars. People who are passionate about tackling climate change and those that are against it both can come up with reasons to decry electric vehicles. They’ll point to the damage of mining the lithium required for the batteries, that public transport is better for the environment than any personal vehicle, or that buying an old combustion engine car avoids the emissions of manufacturing a new electric one. And there are merits to some of these arguments, and things that should be addressed. Public transport could be improved and that would have big climate benefits, mining should be done in the least environmentally damaging way, and there are emissions involved in making a new car. But when it comes down to it, in the long-term electric cars are far better for the climate than regular cars. To Hannah’s point before, they also help reduce air pollution. And we live in a world where cars are integral to many people’s lives, so if people need to drive isn’t a better alternative, better than no alternative?

Hannah also thinks that making viable alternatives for people is going to key in the fight against climate change.

Hannah Ritchie: We could sit here and say well people should just do this because they should just care about the climate and reducing their emissions. And I think lots of people do have that motivation but I think we also need to engage with the fact that people make decisions based on other factors or actually are limited by other factors. Other factors such as cost and affordability, other factors such as availability. So they're kind of forced into the position that they're in. But I think having very good affordable substitutes for people to switch to is just really, really crucial.

Nick Petrić Howe: For those of you that tuned into the previous episode, you’ll know that one of the biggest reasons for optimism when it comes to climate change is due to the energy transition — people using more renewable energy. And the reason for that is that it’s a cheaper alternative to fossil fuels. That hasn’t happened by accident, decades of research into technology like solar energy with the backing of governments to use more renewable energy has pushed down prices. But it underlines Hannah’s point — that when there is a better, and cheaper, alternative available people will use it.

This could also speak to the synergies that Hannah talked about. Cheap, renewable energy could also lift many people out of poverty and could provide power locally, rather than relying on expensive imports of fossil fuels.

And this was one of the most positive aspects of Hannah’s book to me. In the past, I’d always kinda assumed that if we want to improve people’s lives across the world, eliminating poverty and giving people access to all the luxuries I see as commonplace, we’d need to rely on fossil fuels to a certain extent. That’s the way it had worked in the past after all. In the UK, we had the industrial revolution, in China they became the manufacturing centre of the world — both of these transitions relied on fossil fuels. But Hannah thinks that it doesn’t have to be like this anymore.

Hannah Ritchie: I don't think that's as much of a dilemma anymore. We do not need to build out energy and provide people with energy services and the positive things that that brings with fossil fuels anymore. We have viable, affordable, increasingly good alternatives to that.

Nick Petrić Howe: You can see this playing out right now in India. According to the International Energy Agency, India is on track to become one of the biggest markets for renewables and is the government there is expanding its support for rooftop solar projects. And across Africa, where many people live on under a dollar a day, clean energy investments have doubled in recent years, as policies increasing look to make renewable energy part of the mix. Trends which are set to continue as prices for renewable energy keep falling.

Nick Petrić Howe: None of this is exactly straightforward, but what I got from my conversation with Hannah is that there are solutions out there and by looking at the data we can find ways to solve some of them at the same time. Rather than 100 solutions for a hundred problems, maybe we can find a few solutions that meet a few goals at once.

And part of that will involve creating alternatives that people actually want and can make their lives better. Renewable energy makes sense for a lot of people, especially as costs have tumbled.

And Hannah was pretty optimistic overall. Even after spending years looking at the, sometimes bleak, data on climate, she does believe that we can create a better and more sustainable world. There was one aspect, that often comes up in discussions of climate, that she was a bit more pessimistic about.

Hannah Ritchie: I'm relatively sceptical that large amounts of people shift to a more plant-based diet

Nick Petrić Howe: But perhaps there’s a lesson from renewable energy here too.

Bruce Friedrich: About a decade ago, it occurred to me and others that we could take a page from energy transition. And instead of trying to convince the whole world to eat less meat, maybe we can remake meat instead.

Nick Petrić Howe: Continuing my theme of small confessions throughout this series. I have another. I love meat.

I like cooking it. I like the smell of it. Most of all, I like to eat it. Now, maybe that doesn’t sound like much of a confession — I’m in good company, most people around the world eat meat to some degree. But, if you know the environmental concerns around meat, then you’ll know why this is a confession.

Basically, meat leads to a lot more carbon emissions than the alternative of eating plants or plant-based products. That comes down to simple physics. Animals eat plants, and then we eat the animals. Energy is lost through that process and so it is less efficient that you and I just going straight to the source of that energy — eating the plants themselves that have captured the sun’s light. There's a bit more to it than that, but on the face of it eating meat is just less efficient than eating a plant.

That inefficiency leads to warming emissions, with the world Food and Agricultural Organisation (the FAO) estimating that around 15% of global emissions coming from livestock.

And as someone growing up worrying about the climate, I knew this and became a vegetarian because of it. I kept it up through most of my twenties, somewhat successfully. There was the occasional burger I must admit, as like I said, I love meat, so this wasn’t an easy life choice to make. In fact it was so hard that, after losing some weight to an illness, I stopped.

Now I eat meat sparingly, but I do still eat it. Something that I feel guilty about. So, when I got an email about a book suggesting that rather than trying to change how much humans love meat we could change the way it’s produced to cut its climate cost, my interest was piqued.

Bruce Friedrich: In the book, I focus on plant-based meat and cultivated meat.

This is Bruce Fredreich, the founder of the Global Food Institute, a climate nonprofit that seeks to figure out how to make alternatives to meat.

Bruce Friedrich: And the idea of plant-based meat is to say, look, meat is made up of fats, proteins, minerals, and water. Plants also have fats, proteins, minerals, and water. What would it look like to use science to reconstitute plants such that they were indistinguishable from animal meat? And then with cultivated meat, really is as simple as let's take the science of tissue engineering, apply it to meat, which means we can have food grade systems, food grade ingredients, food grade manufacturing and scale it up.

Nick Petrić Howe: I’ll hasten to point out that Bruce is the first to admit that this isn’t that simple, but he makes the case that it can be done, and we are getting closer to that. And if we can get the costs down, then he thinks many people would happily switch to eat these alternatives to meat. Recent polling backs him up. Nearly half of Britons between the ages of 16 and 29 say they would eat lab grown meat — those numbers do decline as people get older, but they point to a common theme. Generally younger people are more willing to eat cultivated or plant-based meat and nearly two thirds of Americans say they would be willing to reduce their meat consumption — even though that consumption has stayed the same so far.

So, the willingness may be there. According to Bruce, if we give people alternatives that taste just as good and are as cheap, if not cheaper than meat, that willingness may finally cause the dietary shift that climate scientists have long hoped for. That’s the big idea that Bruce has dedicated the past decade to. On founding the Global Food Institute he’s been dedicated to figuring out how to make alternative meats that taste and cost the same as the original.

Now, if you follow the science of alternative meats, you may be feeling a little sceptical. I know I was. As much as I wanted to believe in what Bruce was telling me, I feel like I’ve heard that cultivated meat has been about 10 years away for a long time now, and while plant-based meat is more mature — you can go buy it in the supermarket — it doesn’t really taste like meat.

Bruce acknowledges that there are challenges, but he’s optimistic.

Bruce Friedrich: Well I mean I think we overcome the big challenges in the same way that we overcome any other big challenge that's based in science, which is as many people as possible focused on solving the key challenges that we're going to have to solve to get to taste and price parity. That's going to be true on the plant-based side. It's also going to be true on the cultivated side. I talk about this in the book, but one of the things I found most surprising is that the challenge of cultivated meat is significantly more straightforward than the challenge of plant-based meat. The challenge of plant-based meat, it's difficult to get plant fats and proteins to behave like animal fats and proteins. And all over the world, any place you've got a tissue engineering department at a university or anybody working on tissue engineering, all of those people have the basic skill set to solve the cultivated meat scientific challenges. But up until a decade ago, nobody had really tried to figure out how to make plant fats and proteins behave like animal fats and proteins. There's just not another use case for it other than plant-based meat. So it might be scientifically, I mean, it might be scientifically simpler, but there are far fewer people working on the challenge. So in the book, I talk about the fact that we need to change that.

Nick Petrić Howe: With enough people working on the problem, Bruce thinks we can solve it. Maybe not tomorrow, or even soon, but it certainly is possible. But to get enough people working on the problem we have to talk about the dreaded F word. Funding.

On that though, Bruce points out that in recent years governments have started taking quite a lot of notice of this. But they're not typically motivated by climate concerns, instead they're looking to create a cheaper and more reliable food system.

Bruce Friedrich: And this just makes intuitive sense. If you want to raise a chicken for food — and chickens are the most efficient animals at turning crops into meat — it's going to take you in your best-case scenario about nine calories fed to a chicken to get one calorie back out from the chicken. And what that means is that for countries that do not have high food self-sufficiency ratios, they are importing vast amounts of feed crops and they're importing a lot of meat. This is particularly true for China, which when it joined the WTO about 25 years ago was food self-sufficient. Now its food self-sufficiency ratio is down around 70 % and they don't like that. They do not want to be dependent on a global marketplace to feed themselves. This is even more true for countries like Korea, Japan, Singapore, Israel, that are even smaller and have even lower food self-sufficiency ratios. And that and the economic benefits is the reason that governments are enthusiastic about this intervention.

Nick Petrić Howe:This taps a little into what Hannah was saying earlier. One way to tackle climate change is to combine with other problems. Here, promoting self-sufficiency may make governments take notice, and it would come with a climate co-benefit. This isn’t the only advantage of these alt meats.

One of science’s greatest challenges, apart from climate change, is antimicrobial resistance. This is where things like bacteria, viruses and fungi become resistant to he medicines we have to fight them. And meat is not innocent here either.

Antibiotics are often given to healthy animals as it can promote their growth, but this is the exact kind of overuse of antibiotics that scientists have long been warning against as it can lead to antimicrobial resistance.

Bruce suggests that alternative meats, by cutting out animals from the production, could avoid this particular ticking time bomb. Also, for people who worry about the morality of eating animals, having a tasty alternative grown from cells or plants, could help them have their meat and eat it too.

But there are some big hurdles to overcome, before we're all tucking in to our fake meat of choice. Currently, lab-grown meat is prohibitively expensive. And plant-based meat has been tricky to make taste like the real thing, which may put some would-be consumers off. Bruce acknowledges that there’s a far way to go, but he also points to the progress that’s already been made. In 2013, the first lab-grown meat burger was eaten. That cost Sergey Brin, one of Google’s cofounders, 250,000 euros, or around 330,000 US dollars. Today, you can buy cultivated salmon on bagel in Portland, Oregon for $24. And Bruce estimates that a cultivated burger would cost around twice the price of a regular one. As prices tumble, Bruce hopes it’ll encourage more people — vegetarians and meat lovers both — to eat alternative proteins.

He likens the challenge of reimagining meat to that of the energy transition. With enough effort to make a tasty and cheap alternative, more and more people will make the switch.

Bruce Friedrich: So I just find it remarkable that there have been multiple journalists, smart people, who have written about plant-based meat that because it is still too expensive and not good enough, it has failed. As though because we haven't done it yet. We're never ever going to be able to do it. And then uncultivated meat people will say well gosh we put three billion dollars into this. You know where's my cultivated burger? Without thinking about what scientific progress looks like in the context of literally everything else that's ever been done. So three billion dollars across 100 companies and all of time, which is a decade, that's not very long and that's not very much money.

Nick Petrić Howe: In fact, Bruce thinks that if we’re going to make meaningful progress towards our climate goals such action will be essential, especially as meat consumption keeps trending upwards.

Bruce Friedrich: On the climate front, it's literally impossible. On the deforestation and biodiversity front, probably also impossible. What do you think might change that massive upward trajectory? And nobody has an answer. Nobody thinks that after 50 years of trying, we're suddenly going to convince people to eat less meat. But what we can do is make the meat better. And it's not a silver bullet. We need all of the tools in the toolkit. But just like energy transition and electric vehicles are not a silver bullet, but we do need them, the same thing is true here.

Nick Petrić Howe: And a shift to alternative meats could have big benefits. According to a 2023 study, a 50% shift from meat to alternative proteins could net as much benefit as removing the emissions from transport, buildings and aviation put together.

Nick Petrić Howe: Again, this isn’t an easy solution — there are no easy solutions — but if we want to make good on our climate ambitions, the current trajectory of meat eating needs to change. And giving people — especially people like me, who care, but struggle to make the commitment — an alternative, may be a way to temper meat consumption’s rise.

But if we’re talking about alternatives, do we need to think a bit bigger? In a world where society needs to reduce its emissions, but the economic growth that drives that society is fuelled by carbon, is it time to change our economics?

Eoin McLaughlin: How do we save the world? Better measures of the economy.

Nick Petrić Howe: If we want to tackle climate change, and if you’ve listened this far into the podcast then I reckon you do, we’ll have to wrestle with economics. And I know what some people will be saying we just need to get rid of this capitalist system. I too, have been in smoky student houses at 3am, where we’ve also come to this stunning conclusion. But I think reimaging the entire world economic order is probably more than I can do in the space of this podcast. So, we have to do the hard work of thinking about how we can tweak our current system.

As there is a nugget of truth that comes from those bold student statements. The economic systems we have, have historically focused on growth and that ‘growth at any cost’ comes at well… a cost to the climate. So, many scholars agree that there is some reimagining to be done. At the same time, the current system has helped millions out of poverty. So, we’re left with the tricky proposition of solving climate change and making a better world for our descendants. How do economists think about this? With measures.

One big idea is to move beyond one of the world’s favourite economic metrics: Gross Domestic Product — GDP to its friends. This metric gives politicians and observers quick insights every quarter on economic activity of a country — it’s the total market value of the goods and services of a nation in a specific time-window. It’s the number that makes headlines, with politicians clapping themselves on the back or starting to sweat depending on what it says and their party affiliation. And it gives you a rough idea of how a country is doing. A very negative GDP probably spells some trouble at home.

But it’s also something that’s been widely criticized, especially on the climate front. As you could, for example, raise your GDP by cutting every tree down in your country, burning them for energy, exporting them and selling the products from them. While that may give your metrics a boost, you can maybe see why it wouldn’t be the best for the climate.

Eoin McLaughlin: So like GDP doesn't tell us anything about inequality. It doesn't tell us anything about, you know, the state of the planet.

Nick Petrić Howe: This is Eoin McLaughlin, an economist who’s been investigating an alternative to GDP. He thinks a good place to start is with inclusive wealth.

Eoin McLaughlin: So inclusive wealth is supposed to be all the assets that make up the wealth of the country, right? So you think in terms of produced capital, which is all the buildings, machinery, software that we have, all the infrastructure. Then you look at the natural capital that's supposed to be all the natural capital, so fossil fuels, minerals, ecosystems, fisheries, waters, etc. And then human capital, which is the value of knowledge and skill of the population.

Nick Petrić Howe: What inclusive wealth does is allows you to understand whether the current growth of a country is down to building wealth — by doing things like giving people skills to do advanced jobs, investing in infrastructure, and preserving the environment — or whether that wealth is being eroded — by not investing in education, letting bridges and roads fall into decay, and destroying the natural assets, like forests, of a country. These things would put future people’s wealth and prosperity in jeopardy.

On the climate change front, if you include the costs and damages of warming emissions, you can see how wealth is being taken away from future generations, as they have to deal with increasing severity of natural disasters, more difficulty growing crops and rising seas.

Eoin McLaughlin: It basically tells you what's going on, right? If you don't have this and if you're not recording what's going on, you might see, okay, we're growing our economy, but I'm actually running down the natural capital to grow it in the short run. But in the long run, like what's going to happen? You don't really know because you're kind of flying blind. This is a better way to understand what's happening to all the assets in the economy and keep an eye on different things.

Nick Petrić Howe: Eoin isn’t the only one to be thinking about alternatives to GDP. This year a United Nations group of economists came up with a set of recommendations for moving beyond GDP, they suggested that there should be a dashboard of indicators that altogether give a sense of sustainable well-being. Things like life expectancy, air pollution and greenhouse gas emissions.

And in June the World Inequality Lab, a research organization that looks at the drivers of global inequality, called for the richest countries to accept lower growth in order to tackle environmental degradation and climate change.

Both of these have renewed the long running debate on whether nations should stop prioritizing economic growth. As such growth has not helped our climate ambitions or curbed damage to the natural world

But according to Eoin, that’s the wrong question to be asking. Inclusive wealth, to him, tackles whether or not we’re going to leave our descendants poorer or richer.

Eoin McLaughlin: If you really want to know about the long-term wealth of a country, you should be looking at something like inclusive wealth.

Nick Petrić Howe: Eoin explained to me how looking at inclusive wealth may have benefited my own country — the UK. Historically, Britain was one of the leaders of the world economically, now it’s still a wealthy country, but it’s one that didn’t really focus on building wealth for the future.

Eoin McLaughlin: Basically Britain falls behind, right? So it's the leader, pioneer for the Industrial Revolution, like everything starts in Britain, but it falls behind, starting from around 1870, falls behind the United States and Germany. But it falls behind in the industries that require scientific knowledge, the application scientific knowledge, because they don't invest in basic education in Britain. So they're really far behind the United States. The United States is this high school movement. Britain doesn't follow until after the Second World War, effectively. So it's really far behind when it comes to that. And that means you can't thenadopt these new industries and then you start to fall further behind.

This was also true for the UK’s natural resources. Compared to its European neighbours, Britain has little forest cover — at one point only 5% of England had any forest, for example. This not only affects its climate ambitions, but the timber industry too. Realising this, in the first half of the 20th Century, after feeling the effects of few imports during the world wars, the UK moved to reforest the land and invest instead in the future. But it took global crises to think long term.

But that is also the core issue with inclusive wealth. GDP has clung on, despite the criticism, because it’s an easy and quick metric that responds to short-term changes. And as humans we often think short term, you only need to look at climate change for examples to prove that. Whilst we know, as a society, that putting more emissions into the air is going to be bad long-term, we still do it. Partly as the transition is hard, but also because that future is far away, and we have other problems right now. So how do we change our thinking?

Eoin McLaughlin: How do we get people to think about the long-term? We have this thing where people become very pessimistic about the future. They're very you know, they don't really have kind of confidence in the way things are going. And so they've already become disillusioned. So we have to try and bring back some kind of optimism about the future can be good. This is just one way to help us get to a better future.

Nick Petrić Howe: Eoin believes that inclusive wealth can help us build a better future, and not just for climate change. In fact, in his view it’s a mistake to just focus on one thing. Harking back to Hannah’s comments he points out that everything is interrelated and we need to tackle more than one thing at once. And that is a challenge, but perhaps one step is to rethink how we measure the economy. He does still think there is a place for GDP, but amongst other measures. And if we want to save the world, then we need to think about how we measure and make society that we want to live in.

And this idea of making a better society and thinking long-term brings me to something I have a bit of trouble with. We’re already committed to some amount of climate change, in fact, we’re already living in a hotter world. That’s a bit tricky for me to deal with, as I worry about climate change and I worry that we’ve… failed to some extent. But it’s time for me to confront this hotter world. And so we’ve got to think about adaptation.

Susannah Fisher: The way we're currently heading, it's going to affect almost every way that we live our lives, the way we produce food, where people are able to live, how countries relate to each other.

Nick Petrić Howe: So far in this episode, we’ve looked at different big ideas to rein in emissions. We can find synergies to help motivate policymakers to enact change. Why only fix climate change, when you can make us all healthier too? We can offer to alternatives to people, so that the more climate friendly option is also the cost-friendly option. And we can rethink our economies. We don’t necessarily have to change the entire system if we can come up with measures to help people think more long-term. But as we start thinking long-term there’s another reality that we have to face. One that’s often been overlooked when thinking about climate change. Sure, we need to create alternatives and drive down carbon emissions, but how do we adapt to the warming world?

Susannah Fisher: We have unfortunately not managed to reduce greenhouse gas emissions fast enough. So, whatever happens, with stopping burning fossil fuels, we are experiencing damage for the planet, and so we need to respond to that, or the most vulnerable communities and countries are the ones who will bear the brunt.

Nick Petrić Howe: This is Susannah Fisher, a researcher who’s worked with politicians and communities to think more about climate adaptation. Her big idea is that we’re now at an inflexion point, where we will either sink or swim depending on how we tackle adaptation. She wrote a book about it.

Historically, a lot of focus of climate discussions were about how to stop the climate warming. And that’s for good reason — the best way to avoid intense heatwaves, droughts, fires, floods, and destruction is to stop emitting carbon and so prevent as much warming as possible.

But… the climate is going to warm. Even if we were to immediately stop all emissions right this second, we’re committed to at least some amount of warming. So that means we really need to think about how we adapt — how we change the way we live to withstand a warmer world.

Susannah Fisher: With current policy trajectories, it's likely that we might see around 2.5 degrees of global average temperature rises. So that will mean extreme heat in many places, changing rainfall and monsoons, sea level rise, strengthened storms and storm surges. And about 3 billion people are going to be highly vulnerable to those changes.

Nick Petrić Howe: When I first learned about Susannah’s book, it sounded it pretty worrying. As someone who struggles with anxiety about the climate, hearing that there’s the potential we might all ‘sink’ didn’t do wonders for how I felt. But I reached out to Susannah to learn more, and I found that she had a nuanced view. She explained to me that, sure, there are hard choices ahead of us, but opportunities too.

Susannah Fisher: We have got two choices really in the future that's coming up and that agency lies within us. So it's a scenario where we keep going as we are. We don't adapt significantly into climate change and we don't reduce greenhouse gases fast enough. And I call that a sink scenario. That's where things continue and unfortunately vulnerable countries and communities bear the brunt of those risks. Or there's a scenario where we look at those risks right now, we take them seriously, we rethink how we're managing water, droughts, relationships between countries, and we take it as an opportunity to imagine new futures. And for me that would be a swim scenario.

Nick Petrić Howe: Having agency to make a better future certainly sounds more optimistic than I was expecting, because the thing is… adaptation a bit of a tricky topic. This podcast series has focused a lot on optimism, about what we can do and to help people who, like me, might be close to losing hope. So, talking about how we adapt to a warmer climate almost feels like an admission of failure, that we’ve been too slow and haven’t done enough.

But, frankly, I need to go over myself. Adaptation is necessary. I’m not the only one who needs to get over myself though.

These days adaptation is a big area of research and a key part of the negotiations around climate. But historically, it’s been pushed down the agenda. Understandably, researchers and politicians have wanted to focus more on trying to stop climate change in the first place, so discussions of how we adapt to a warmer world were seen as a bit of a distraction in early climate discussions. That has changed in recent years and it’s not like society isn’t adapting. We have walls to defend against rising seas, people have been relocated to avoid floods, or funding for farmers who are facing droughts. But as Susannah explained to me, the changes we’ve seen haven’t really been enough.

Susannah Fisher: Whilst we've got lots of adaptation going on so far, the problem is it's mainly incremental. So, it's mainly addressing the current risks and helping people to live as they are in the places where they currently are. So, whilst we've made important starts, one of the key arguments I wanted to make in the book is actually the impacts that we're going to see are so significant that we're going to need to make this step change in the activity and the way that we do adaptation.

Nick Petrić Howe: Part of the issue, Susannah told me is that people have focused on short-term fixes that may not really pay off in the long-term. Like with the discussion of GDP, politicians tend to get rewarded for short-term changes, rather than longer term investments that may pay dividends as they help us live in a warmer world. That world is a long way off for a politician looking at the next election cycle.

You can think of this way. Air conditioning is an adaptation to a warmer climate; it helps you stay cool as summers get hotter. In a particularly hot spell, a savvy politician may even offer subsidies to fit air conditioning into homes and businesses. But long-term, those air conditioning units may actually drive carbon emissions, making the problem worse. Not to mention all the hot air they spurt out into the outside world. The harder, longer-term, adaptation would be to make city environment cooler. Creating canals that can cool the surrounding area, planting trees along streets to provide shade, and changing building design to cool the area around and in them. These kind of changes require a lot more political will and time, for something that people may not see the benefit of immediately.

Now, air conditioning probably will be part of adaptation, especially in large public areas, to allow people to escape the heat, but they help illustrate the idea that short-term changes are attractive, even if they risk causing more harm in the long-term. And that’s one of the key ideas behind Susannah’s book – there are hard choices ahead.

Susannah Fisher: There are some things that aren't really politically simple. There isn't one clear scientific answer. They actually really depend on what people value, what they want for their future, and involves many different perspectives. And they might also involve trade-offs, short-term political and economic costs for long-term benefit.

Nick Petrić Howe: Politically, as well you will often have the environmental department of a nation proposing adaptation, but they have to compete with the treasury. It’s not hard to see who often wins that fight.

Susannah Fisher: You know, what government would want to take a short-term hit for managing something that could have an upfront economic cost but longer-term economic benefit? It's a real political trade-off between managing those risks.

Nick Petrić Howe: According to Susannah, that means that often governments will do adaptations that just make sense anyway, like changing all the bulbs to be more energy efficient. Sure, that saves energy and therefore helps stop climate warming emissions, but it’s also just cheaper. A nice synergy perhaps, but not really enough to help us adapt to climate change.

As the climate warms, we’ll see much more significant choices ahead of us than lightbulbs. As disasters strike and seas rise, people are going to be forced to move.

Susannah Fisher: So I would want to make sure that we don't go down a kind of a narrative of fear around huge flows of climate-related migration, because climate-related movement is actually much more complex than that. It's really hard to put numbers on the scale of the challenge because it involves a whole load of assumptions. So you'll see numbers between, say, 200 million and over a billion. And it's really down to how you assume that climate change plays out, but also the policies in place.

Nick Petrić Howe: Most climate migration has been, and likely will be, within countries, rather than between them. In the US, for example, millions of people have already moved to escape flooding in the past 20 years, not all of that will be down to climate change, but as the planet warms flooding is projected to get worse. And some cities in the US, like Buffalo, New York, have start advertising themselves as climate refuges — places where people can come and be free from drought, heat and other disasters.

Even when people do cross borders, those movements tend to be to close countries. But as the climate gets warmer, Susannah thinks we need to think hard about how we manage this.

Susannah Fisher: And so what's really important is how do we facilitate that as an adaptation strategy? I think not just about the people who might need to go for a variety of reasons, of which climate is one, but also the places that those people go. Like what does it mean to host people well, to find space for people, to provide services for people so that the whole trajectory of any potential climate related migration is supported.

Nick Petrić Howe: And I don’t have to go far to see how this might play out. In the UK, millions of people may be at risk of coastal flooding, and so may have to move. Most of that will likely be to places in the UK, but the question is, where should they go? And what will happen to their communities.

I had hoped that Susannah had some answers to these questions. I ask everyone I talk to ‘how to save world?’, I desperately want to know what the path forward is.

But her point is that there are hard choices ahead of us, and we all need to think carefully about the world we want to make. People moving is only one part of this too, we need to think about how to adapt crops, deal with the effects on wild animals and plants, and manage conflict in a warmer world.

This may all sound a bit overwhelming, I know it did to me as I was reading Susannah’s book. There’s a lot of difficult choices ahead of us, and, so far, limited progress. But Susannah focuses on the opportunities that are there too.

Susannah Fisher: So one can often feel downhearted with the climate crisis, unsure where to find hope and optimism. And I think the important thing is that we look at the future that we want to build for ourselves, for our families, for our communities, and for global relationships. And we think, what is our role in creating that? And I think it's important to hold on to the hope and hold on to the next step, that we've all got the chance to make change where we are, and that is how we're going to adapt to climate change and build the world that we want to live in.

Nick Petrić Howe: Climate change is a big, scary problem. So, I’m glad that there are people out there who also have big ideas on how to fix it. We can find fixes to multiple problems at once, maybe we can finally end humanity’s addiction to meat, and we can perhaps nudge our economies in a way that makes more long-term sense for the climate. At the same time, we’ll need to adapt to the warmer world we’ve committed to. That’ll mean making some hard choices, but the longer it is until we make them, the harder they’ll get.

The ideas we’ve discussed here are by no means an exhaustive list. There are so many people working on climate change, and so many ideas on what to do about it. We haven’t talked about carbon taxes, for instance, where climate is costed in — something which a lot of evidence supports, even if politicians are a bit more wary. Or heck, if you want a really big idea, there’s geoengineering, but that is a difficult thing to test and there’s a lot of unintended consequences that could come with it. And there’s methane too, efforts to stop this particularly greenhouse gas leaking out could make a sizeable dent in reining in climate change. Maybe you have a big idea of your own. As Susannah alluded to, we’ll need all of us to come together to try and solve this big problem.

But as I bring this episode to a close, I still have Susannah’s last words ringing in my head. That we’ve all got a role to play in making the world we want to live in. So far, I’ve been pleasantly surprised by where the data say we’re at in terms of climate change, and I’ve optimistic that some of these ideas out that can maybe help, but I still feel a bit lost myself. The scale of the problem seems overwhelming, and I’m just one person. And I’m not sure what to do about that. What am I supposed to do with that distress?

But young people are saying, you know, we don't want our distress to be taken away in a sense, because this shows that we care. It shows that we care about the world. It can be fuel for action, and it can be a really good thing

Nick Petrić Howe: Maybe there’s a way I can use it. That’s next time.

This podcast was produced and written by me, Nick Petrić Howe. Dan Fox was my editor. Thanks also to Emma Lawrence, Bruce Friedrich, Eoin McLaughlin, and Susanna Fisher for talking to me for this episode. And thank you for listening.

#1556. ​Arteta’s ‘dynasty’ dream collides with Arsenal’s harsh reality

Mikel Arteta says he wants to create a “dynasty” at Arsenal as he threw down the gauntlet to his players to retain their Premier League title and reach a “different level”.

Arsenal are on the verge of completing a £75m deal for Brazil midfielder Bruno Guimãraes from Newcastle and have not given up hope of landing Real Madrid winger Vinícius Júnior, who has been offered an improved contract by the Spanish giants.

The Premier League champions slumped to a 3-1 defeat to Real Betis in Dublin on Wednesday night, when they paid the price for individual errors and a lethargic, sloppy defensive display.

But that did little to quell Arteta’s ambitions for the new season. “I’m even more excited [about this season], and we’re going to go and attack every possible title because that’s the ambition that we have,” he said.

“We know that we have the ability. We will go from a strength to a strength as well, whether it’s with the players that we have to take them to a different level, and with the market that is still open to recruit as well, so we are very optimistic about it.

“All the work that we’ve done – that I’ve done through the summer – is to understand what we need to do to win again and to create a dynasty in this football club. That’s the aim.”

Despite Arteta’s bullishness, he conceded Arsenal would have to be a lot better than they were against Betis. When asked about the mood in the dressing room, he said: “Very upset, given a hard time. They are fuming, but this is good. That’s what we need.”

Telegraph Sport analyses some of the talking points from a disappointing evening at the Aviva Stadium.

The importance of goalkeeper David Raya and centre-backs William Saliba and Gabriel Magalhães to Arsenal hardly needs overstating. Their title success was built on the foundations provided by that triumvirate at the back.

Raya has yet to report back from holiday after Spain’s World Cup triumph and Saliba is facing an extended spell on the sidelines with a back injury. Gabriel did appear for the second half but, watching this, Arteta is unlikely to have been dissuaded from the belief he needs another top defender to compensate for the loss of Saliba.

It may have been only Arsenal’s second game of pre-season, so a degree of legginess was understandable.

But the ease with which they were cut open and overloaded by the Spanish side, and the volume of individual errors, did not sit comfortably with Arteta with just over a fortnight until they kick off their title defence at home to newly promoted Coventry City.

Only once in 63 matches last season did Arsenal concede three goals in a single game but they were fortunate Betis did not score more. “In the first half there are two different things: to play well and to compete,” said Arteta, who saw his side trail 3-1 at the interval.

“We did the first one quite well in a lot of moments but the compete part – especially in and around our box – was not to the standards to win a football match against a good side. It’s better to give them [the goals away] in a friendly match than an official match. It’s always good when you lose a match in pre-season because it creates a bit more fire in the belly.”

Kepa Arrizabalaga will not want to watch Betis’s first goal back in a hurry. The Arsenal goalkeeper may have got a slight nudge as he came for the ball at a corner but he was all over the place and never looked even in the vaguest control of the situation. Rodrigo Riquelme scored at the far post after the ball sailed over the keeper. Arteta called it a “really sloppy goal”. With former Leeds goalkeeper Illan Meslier having arrived on a free transfer as back-up to Raya, Kepa faces an uncertain future at Arsenal. Moments like this will not help his cause.

He did not feature much last season but is probably best remembered for his torrid showing in the Carabao Cup final defeat by Manchester City in March. He looked as unconvincing here as he did then, as the former Chelsea goalkeeper also sliced a clearance in the build up to Betis’s third goal. Before then, Kai Havertz had turned over possession cheaply from which Nelson Deossa set up former West Ham midfielder Pablo Fornals to score.

Arsenal need more creativity and firepower in attack, hence the interest in Vinícius and Atlético Madrid’s Julián Alvarez. Viktor Gyokeres again looked rather limited here and the likes of Bukayo Saka and Eberechi Eze are also still to report back. Yet one of the few, brighter aspects of Arsenal’s performances was the sight of the regal looking Riccardo Calafiori marauding forward from a very nominal left-back role.

If Arsenal are going to play more adventurously this season and try to ratchet up things in the entertainment stakes then Calafiori could have a big role to play, as long as Arteta can keep him fit. He can be a potent weapon galloping forward and there were clear glimpses of that here. Harnessing that talent while not compromising too much defensive security may be one of the manager’s challenges.

Louie Copley had only been on the pitch for nine minutes – a half-time substitute for Ben White – when the 19-year-old midfielder went down largely unchallenged with what looked like a troubling knee injury. Arteta admitted afterwards that the way the teenager fell to the ground was a concern and he looked in visible pain and distress as he was treated by the medical staff before being helped off the pitch.

The fear will be of some kind of ligament damage and Arteta confirmed Copley would be scanned on Thursday. “Quite worried to be fair for the kid because the mechanism doesn’t look very positive and the symptoms that he already has,” the manager said. “So we are going to have to wait and see for tomorrow’s scan. Touch wood that is not a bad one.”

“It is another opportunity for fitness. Coming into games against teams of good quality, it is important we get good fitness. It is a chance to build momentum for the season ahead. We are taking steps in the right direction. Of course, we want more from the performance and the results, but we take learnings and move on.

“All of us, together, we share a common goal. We have confidence to build on. We will take every game as it comes. The atmosphere was amazing. I did not realise Ireland has so many Arsenal fans. We are so grateful for everyone who came to support us today. We wanted to give them a good result and performance. Hopefully next time we can.”

“We always want to win and in the end we could not today. In some ways they deserved it and we could have done better. We did have some good moments though. We had an amazing season last season. I believe in this team and there are still players to come back from the World Cup. I am confident but we can always do better.”

There is the final whistle in Dublin and Betis secure a 3-1 win over Arsenal at Aviva Stadium. Goals from Riquelme, Deossa and Fornals has led Manuel Pellegrini’s side to the victory. All four goals in the game came before the break.

And that's full time in Dublin 👏Real Betis claim a 3-1 win against Premier League champions Arsenal 🌴 pic.twitter.com/0XWByNdtgh

Jesus gets onto the end of a ball in behind, getting to it just before the byline, and delivers a dangerous cross but Natan does well on the stretch to clear.

Antony was booed when he came on and is also being booed whenever he touches the ball.

Arsenal have registered just two shots on target in this game and both of those came in the first half. They have not really looked like scoring since the break, with probably Jesus coming closest.

Double change for Betis as Morante and Gomez replace Riquelme and Bernal.

Bellerin squares the ball from the byline and picks out Riquelme near the penalty spot but the latter is unable to take advantage.

The changes keep coming for Arsenal as Gabriel and Martinelli, who have only recently returned from their breaks after the World Cup, go off after half an hour on the pitch. Nwaneri was the final member of the Arsenal starting XI to still be on but his night is over.

Up until this point, Manuel Pellegrini had made just one change but he now makes a triple substitution, which sees three former Premier League players come on. Former Leeds duo Firpo and Llorente come on as does ex-Manchester United forward Antony. There are a few boos from the Arsenal fans as Antony comes on.

Martinelli is played in down the left channel and gets onto the end of the ball inside the Betis box. He checks back and finds his compatriot Jesus on the edge of the box. Jesus tries to pick out the bottom corner but his shot goes just wide.

Isco should put Betis 4-1 up but tries to be too cute and clever. Former Arsenal man Bellerin delivers a cross from the right side of the box and picks out a free Isco in the six-yard box. Isco attempts an audacious flick rather than putting his foot through it and his effort is saved by Meslier. That should have been a goal.

Arsenal have changed nearly their entire starting XI whereas Betis have made just the one substitution thus far. Betis have played more games so far in pre-season, which probably explains the difference in the number of changes.

Salmon is deceived by a dummy by Riquelme and then brings the Betis man down, earning him a yellow card.

On the hour mark, Mikel Arteta is going to make a triple change, which feels like it was a plan going into the game. That includes Meslier coming on in goal in place of Kepa.

Copley is helped off by the two Arsenal medics, shaking his head and not putting any weight on his left leg, and is replaced by Julienne.

You have to hope that the knee injury to Louie Copley is not serious but judging by the way he went down largely unchallenged, his reaction and the way he was being helped down the tunnel it didn’t look too good. A tough moment for the youngster who had only been on the pitch nine minutes.

Play is halted as Copley has been down for a little while clutching at his left knee. He got his studs stuck in the ground and went down in some pain. The medics come on to check that left knee. He only came on at half-time but his night is over not even 10 minutes into the second half.

Nwaneri catches Bernal and if this was a competitive fixture than I think Nwaneri would perhaps have been booked for that challenge.

Those raft of changes from Mikel Arteta at half-time have seen just four of their starting XI remain on the pitch; Kepa, Calafiori, Lewis-Skelly and Nwaneri.

Arsenal have a corner early on in this second half as Vieira’s shot from distance deflects behind. The delivery from the left has too much on it, going over the heads of all the Arsenal players in the box, and Betis are able to clear.

Mikel Arteta has made a whole host of changes, which includes the likes of Jesus, Martinelli, Gabriel and Vieira coming on. Betis have brought the former Real Madrid man Isco on at the break.

Possession: Arsenal 63%-37% Real BetisShots: 5-7Shots on target: 2-6Corners: 1-2

Arsenal’s title triumph was built on that stout defence and conceding so few but there have been so many self-inflicted wounds here. The first and third goals came from dismal individual errors from Kepa and Havertz and the second - while a wonder strike - came after Arsenal had failed to clear their lines properly.

The first half is brought to an end and Real Betis take a 3-1 lead into the break.

Manuel Pellegrini’s side have their third goal of the night and restore their two-goal advantage. Havertz gives the ball away poorly deep inside his own half and the ball is played into Fornals. The former West Ham man has it on the edge of the box and has P Garcia in space to his right but opts to shoot. It is a clinical finish from Fornals as he picks out the bottom left corner and celebrates by crossing his arms to form irons, paying tribute to his days at West Ham.

"It's so so easy!" 🎙️The former West Ham man Pablo Fornals puts Real Betis 3-1 up against Arsenal 🌴🔨 pic.twitter.com/iyBeyS1nHd

Betis come close to restoring their two-goal advantage. Calafiori gives the ball away deep inside his own half and the ball is quickly moved onto P Garcia on the right side of the box. He opens up his body and curls a shot first time towards the far corner, forcing Kepa into the save down to his right.

Riquelme shoots from just outside the box and forces Kepa into a save down to his right.

Betis have one goal from a corner and now Arsenal do. Betis keeper Valles complains that he is being fouled by Havertz after Tzolis swung in the corner from the left and the ball comes through to Hincapie, who has the simplest of headers from inside the six-yard box.

Normal service is resumed with a Gunners goal from the corner 👏Piero Hincapié gives the @Arsenal fans reason to celebrate! 🔴 pic.twitter.com/b7h979i0Gv

Important block from P Garcia. Dowman cuts in from the right across the face of the penalty area and finds Tzolis in space to his left. Tzolis takes one touch before taking on the shot from inside the Betis box but P Garcia slides in with a crucial block.

That is quite the finish! Deossa receives the ball in a central position around 25 yards out. He takes a couple of touches before lashing a shot with his left foot. His effort flies into the top corner and Betis have a 2-0 lead. Considering the quality of the finish, I am surprised that Deossa did not celebrate more bearing in mind you do not score screamers like that every day!

Nelson Deossa...what a hit! 😱😱Real Betis double their lead over Arsenal with a stunning strike and Mikel Arteta doesn't look happy 🌴 pic.twitter.com/4J5QnjOury

Since Gyokeres misses that very good chance just a minute into the game, Arsenal have not really carved out many genuine opportunities in front of goal, other than that Tzolis wasted chance. Every time they reach the final third, they are lacking that cutting edge.

Calafiori’s role is interesting. He’s very nominally a left back but is routinely stepping into midfield and raiding forward, often ending up in positions you’d associate with a No. 10. It’s the kind of role Nico O’Reilly played under Pep Guardiola at Manchester City.

Valles is so, so lucky. The Betis keeper inexplicably passes the ball straight at Tzolis inside the Betis penalty area but Tzolis is unable to capitalise. That is a huge slice of luck for Valles as that was a ridiculous moment.

Betis have already scored one goal from a corner and they now have another corner after Nwaneri’s clearance behind. The inswinger is sent into a good area but this time Arsenal deal with the danger.

Arsenal were the better side in the early stages but Betis have grown into this and have taken confidence from that goal.

The first goal of the night goes the way of the Spaniards. The corner from the left should be dealt with by Kepa but the Arsenal keeper makes an absolute mess of it. The ball goes straight through him and comes to Riquelme at the far post. He takes one touch before firing into the net. Kepa is appealing for a free-kick but there is never a foul in there.

Real Betis strike first at the Aviva! 🌴Riquelme takes advantage of poor Arsenal defending at the corner to open the scoring 👀 pic.twitter.com/1ubVDayElP

That is dire goalkeeping from Kepa. He’s desperately tried to claim he was fouled but he just made a complete hash of it.

Betis have their first shot of the night. P Garcia receives it out on the right and cuts inside onto his left. The space opens up for him to shoot and he obliges, forcing Kepa into a save before the ball is smashed behind for a corner...

Calafiori may be on the teamsheet tonight for Arsenal at left-back but when they are in possession the Italian is moving into midfield. Lewis-Skelly, who is playing in the number six role, is dropping in between the two centre-backs when Arsenal have the ball.

Betis win a free-kick out on the left, with the chance to send it into the Arsenal penalty area for the first time tonight. It is clipped into a good area but Kepa is out of his goal to catch it.

Arsenal should be ahead one minute into the game with their first attack of the game. Havertz picks up the ball on the corner of the box out on the left and passes it inside to Gyokeres. The Swedish striker takes one touch before shooting from the edge of the six-yard box but his shot is saved. In reality, Gyokeres should not have given Valles in the Betis goal any chance of saving that one.

Both sides emerge from the tunnel, Arsenal led out by Ben White and Betis by former Arsenal man Hector Bellerin, and make their way past the Premier League trophy. We are moments away from kick-off in Dublin.

Arsenal: Kepa; White, Mosquera, Hincapie, Calafiori; Lewis-Skelly, Havertz, Nwaneri; Dowman, Gyokeres, Tzolis.

“When I see the training and how hungry they are for every training drill, that means everybody is ready to compete at the highest level. When you are a player of Arsenal, you compete for every title that is possible. It is not only about the Premier League, it is about all the competitions we are playing for. I see a clear mindset and everything, that everybody is on the same page to win titles here. I saw it from the first training and I think when you train like that in the game, it makes it even better. I came here ready, with my fitness level and I was happy that I could show it here as well. I want to be myself and to show on the pitch all the passion and desire to win because I really like to win games and to give everything.

“If I give 100% for every game and every duel, I think who does not like this? I think that is the best thing for a football player, and then you will always have the support from the supporters. I am thinking about how to improve and settle as fast as possible in the club, because I have the opportunity to train directly with the team from the beginning of the season, to play pre-season games and then to go to official games. This is a chance to play directly from the beginning and then it is up to me to show the qualities and what I can bring to the team. I am pretty confident I will show it in the next games.”

Arsenal are closing in on the signing of Newcastle and Brazil midfielder Bruno Guimaraes in a deal worth £75m. He has been given permission to undergo a medical today and is set to join Arsenal in the coming days. One midfielder coming into Arsenal is set to see another depart as Dane Christian Norgaard closes in on a move to Everton after just one season at Arsenal.

Our starting XI for #ArsenalRealBetis! 💚🤍 pic.twitter.com/8rRvy9IZCm

Premier League champions Arsenal continue their preparations for the new season as they take on Spanish side Real Betis at the Aviva Stadium in Dublin, with this being the first-ever meeting between the two sides. This is the first time Arsenal have played a pre-season game in Dublin since August 2018, when they drew 1-1 with London rivals Chelsea, with Arsenal winning on penalties.

Arsenal beat Girona 4-1 in their opening game of pre-season, with new signing Christos Tzolis on the scoresheet in his first appearance for the club. After today, Arsenal have three more games, including the Community Shield, before they kick off the defence of their Premier League crown at home against newly-promoted Coventry on opening night of the new season. They are closing in on a deal for Newcastle captain Bruno Guimaraes, who is set to become one of Arsenal’s most expensive signings. Mikel Arteta’s side have been dealt a blow ahead of the season with the news that France centre-back William Saliba will miss an extended period due to a back injury. The likes of Declan Rice, Bukayo Saka and Noni Madueke are still yet to return after their World Cup exploits.

Real Betis, under the management of former Manchester City boss Manuel Pellegrini, finished fifth in La Liga last season and have therefore qualified for this coming season’s Champions League after a 20-year absence from the competition. Pellegrini has led Betis into European competitions for five consecutive seasons, which includes losing the 2025 Europa Conference League final to Chelsea. They have been busy in pre-season action already having played five games up to this point. They have won four of the five, including a 4-0 victory over Lyon, with just one defeat coming against Granada.

They have a number of former Premier League players in their ranks, including Antony, Giovani Lo Celso, Pablo Fornals and former Arsenal man Hector Bellerin. Real Betis have already played a number of friendlies as they build up to the start of their season, which begins on August 21 when they take on Real Sociedad.

#1555. SCOTLAND 2 NORTH MACEDONIA 1: John McGinn at the double to spare the blushes of Pocognoli's shaky Scots on skipper Robertson's big night

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER

Published: 17:01 EST, 13 November 2026 | Updated: 17:11 EST, 13 November 2026

On the night when the nation looked over its shoulder and celebrated the past, the here and now for Scotland looked distinctly uncertain.

Coming 40 years and a day after his friend, Sir Kenny Dalglish, pulled on a Scotland jersey for the 102nd and final time, Andy Robertson joined the great man on a mark which, for years, seemed beyond the reach of mere mortals.

By time up, history had mercifully repeated itself at Hampden. Back in the day, Dalglish, by then player-manager at Anfield, sailed into the international sunset on the back of a routine 3-0 win over Luxembourg.

Facing another opponent of modest ability, Robertson’s red letter day didn’t go quite as smoothly. Yet, when the Tottenham man is old and grey and reflecting on the night he created history, the annals will at least record a slender victory.

While his side did just about enough to prevail here, this was another fraught night for Sebastien Pocognoli.

You can talk about the need for patience under the new manager until the cows come home. But North Macedonia are 71st in FIFA’s rankings. Scotland are 43rd.

John McGinn celebrates in trademark fashion after netting Scotland's winner from the spot

At Hampden Park, in front of an expectant crowd, Scotland should be putting them to the sword with something to spare.

Yet, for long enough, the Belgian’s new-look side were flat, predictable and plodding. It said much that it took the intervention of VAR for them to get the penalty which would ultimately lead to three points being accrued.

John McGinn’s second half double saved the Belgian’s blushes and truthfully there was little else to get the Tartan Army off their seats.

Too many big-name players scarcely merited pass marks. Too few looked comfortable in the system the manager is trying to bed in.

If it was a step in the right direction, it was a small one. After five games under the affable Belgian, the progress has certainly not been startling.

While it goes without saying that beating the Swiss in St Gallen on Monday will be an inordinately tougher task, having some hope of moving up a place and securing a kinder draw for the Euros is still better than no hope.

Regardless of what pot they end up in when the draw is made in Belfast next month, a radical improvement will certainly be required across the board if they are to stand any chance of qualifying for the tournament via the front door.

As well as the achievements of Robertson and Dalglish, the career of Craig Gordon was acknowledged before the match with the 84-times capped keeper deservedly afforded a warm hand by the Tartan Army.

McGinn slots home his penalty after Ben Gannon-Doak had been brought down in the area

There were absolutely no excuses for Scotland here. North Macedonia were a tier-two team in name only. They arrived at Hampden having not won in 12 matches and not scored in eight.

Another Pocognoli game saw another back-three combination. This time Luke Graham was selected in the centre of the unit with Ryan Porteous and Kieran Tierney deployed either side of the Stoke man in what were their first appearances under the Belgian.

Robertson and Ben Gannon-Doak were tasked with providing the width in the 3-4-3. Scott McTominay slotted back into an advanced role beside John McGinn with the returning Che Adams asked to lead the line.

For all there was a healthy crowd in excess of 40,000 inside Hampden, the atmosphere was subdued. In the four Nations League games to date under the new manager, the side hadn’t exactly given the supporters much to feed off.

Despite some big guns returning, Scotland made a laboured start to their night’s work. It said much that Graham, on his second appearance, was busier than any defender in white.

The first opening came as a result of an opposition error. John McGinn found Billy Gilmour who fed the overlapping Robertson. The skipper’s cross was well out of Adams’ reach.

Sebastien Pocognoli got his first Hampden win as Scotland boss but it was a nervy night

Although Ljupche Doriev worried Angus Gunn with a curling effort, Scotland began to exert some degree of control on the match. Lewis Ferguson kept the visitors hemmed in with a header into McTominay’s feet. The Napoli man saw his shot on the spin well saved by Stole Dimitrievski.

Pocognoli was frustrated when Slovakian referee Michal Ocenas blew for a foul on McTominay, his justifiable gripe being that playing an advantage would have seen Robertson have a crack at goal.

Dimitrievski had a decent night. Although Adams’ flashing header from McGinn’s corner took a deflection, a reflex save at his near post added to Scotland’s frustration.

North Macedonia were a spirited but ordinary side. They still had enough to thwart Pocognoli’s men.

Gannon-Doak saw plenty of the ball down the right, yet the end product often wasn’t there. The Bournemouth man did tee up Billy Gilmour for one dangerous cross. McTominay tried to replicate his iconic overhead kick against Denmark nearly a year ago. This time, his aim wasn’t true.

You could hardly blame Pocognoli’s star man for failing to find the net on that occasion.

Scott McTominay attempts an overhead spectacular a year on from THAT goal at Hampden

That wasn’t the case a few moments later when Adams slipped him in. Dimitrievski saved McTominay’s strike with an outstretched leg when he should have been picking the ball out of his net.

Adams had just blazed a strike high over the top while one-on-one with the keeper although the offside flag saved his blushes.

The visitors came closer to edging ahead when Eljif Elmas played the pass of the match over Scotland’s static defence to pick out Ezgjan Alioski. His lay-off was smashed into the side net by Enis Bardhi.

A wholly uninspiring first-half concluded with Robertson advancing up the left and launching a cross halfway to Castlemilk. This was not going well.

Pocognoli waited on the edge of the pitch for his players returning, his enthusiastic applause clearly audible in the arena.

His hopes of a breakthrough at the outset of the second period were dashed in extraordinary fashion. Adams did well to chase a ball down to the line and cut it back. McTominay and his marker couldn’t connect, leaving Gilmour the simple task of firing into an unguarded net. Leaning back, his failure to even hit the target was unfathomable.

Elmin Rastoder celebrates after silencing Hampden with a leveller for North Macedonia

Within seconds, the sense of relief inside Hampden was palpable as the opener finally arrived. Porteous got enough distance on his clearing header for Adams to barge Visar Musliu out of the way.

McGinn was alert to the situation and burst into the box. His crisp strike finally had the beating of the goalkeeper.

It should have settled Pocognoli’s side and paved the way for a comfortable result. Instead, they were pegged back within three minutes.

It was all just so simple and so avoidable. Bardhi’s whipped corner only needed McTominay to outjump his man. Flat-footed as the delivery arrived, he could only watch on in horror as Elmin Rastoder’s flashing header beat Angus Gunn.

Although Gilmour worked the keeper with a low strike, North Macedonia also sniffed a second goal. Time and time again, they got into pockets of space on the flanks and fired in dangerous crosses.

Adams made way for Oli McBurnie, the Hull man desperately hoping for his first goal on his 21st international appearance. He had a gilt-edged chance to get off the mark when rolled in by McGinn, but selflessly passed to the overlapping Gannon-Doak.

Scotland move on to their final game away in Switzerland as they look to finish on a high note

The winger appeared to take a heavy touch which allowed the keeper to rescue the situation. VAR, however, spotted that Dimitrievski had impeded him. Penalty.

McGinn did the necessary from 12 yards, smashing the ball straight down the middle for his 24th international goal.

North Macedonia, to their credit, kept going for it. They sensed a fragility in Scotland. Everyone in the ground could.

McGinn’s calm conversion proved to be just about enough to get the job done. But it’s fair to suggest that we are still awaiting lift-off in the new era.

SCOTLAND (3-4-1-2): Gunn; Porteous, Graham, Tierney; Gannon-Doak (Hickey 76), Ferguson, Gilmour (Christie 76), Robertson; McGinn; Adams (McBurnie 67), McTominay. Booked: Ferguson. Manager: Sebastien Pocognoli.

NORTH MACEDONIA (4-2-3-1): Dimitrievski; Ilievski, Mladenovski, Musliu, Alioski; Gashtarov (Elezi 64), Elmas (Stankovski 78); Churlinov (Maleski 64), Bardhi, Doriev (Nikolov 85); Rastoder. Booked: None. Manager: Goce Sedloski.
